findings.title: Race condition in BlockedEmail.should_block?
findings.body: `should_block?` uses a non-atomic read-modify-write to update `match_count` and `last_match_at`. Two concurrent validations can both read the same `match_count`, both increment it in memory, and the second `save` overwrites the first, silently losing increments and clobbering `last_match_at`. Under any real sign-up load (the very load this PR is trying to throttle), statistics for blocked emails will be wrong. Use an atomic update, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now)`, and skip callbacks/validations.

findings.title: record.save runs validations/callbacks for a counter update
findings.body: Calling `record.save` triggers the full ActiveRecord lifecycle (validations including `uniqueness`, callbacks) every time an email is checked, just to bump a counter. If a uniqueness race loses, the in-memory `record` is still returned as truthy in `should_block?`, so the user is blocked while the match counter was never persisted, and the exception is silently swallowed. For pure-statistic writes, use `update_columns`/`update_all` so the outcome isn't tied to a `save` succeeding.

findings.title: Blocked email is not case-normalized; admin and signup inputs must match exactly
findings.body: Both the model and the migration store `email` verbatim (case-sensitive unique index). The new validator compares it case-sensitively, and User#email is set from `params[:email]` without `Email.downcase`, so `Bad@Spam.com` (admin entry) and `bad@spam.com` (signup) are treated as different addresses. A blocklist entry that looks correct in the admin UI can be bypassed by submitting the same address with different casing, or with surrounding whitespace. Normalize via `before_validation` (e.g. `self.email = Email.downcase(email.to_s.strip)`) and consider a case-insensitive index so this can't be bypassed.

findings.title: rejectedEmails.contains is case-sensitive, allowing easy bypass of client-side block
findings.body: `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` does a strict string compare. After the server rejects `Bad@Spam.com`, that exact string is pushed. The user can then re-enter `bad@spam.com` (or add a space); the client validation passes, they resubmit, and only then learn from the server it's blocked. The UX promise of this PR — instant feedback for blocked emails — is broken. Normalize both sides (e.g. `email.toLowerCase()`) before pushing into `rejectedEmails` and before the contains check.

findings.title: Whitelist/blacklist paths were moved from User but have no test coverage
findings.body: The EmailValidator now owns the entire domain whitelist/blacklist logic that previously lived in `User#email_validator`, but the spec only covers the BlockedEmail branch. A regression in the regex construction (e.g. `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` with a comma-separated list — currently `@(gmail\.com,foo\.bar)`, which only matches the literal string `gmail.com,foo.bar`, not either domain) would not be caught. Add specs covering: whitelist allows/disallows, blacklist allows/disallows, comma-separated domains, interaction with BlockedEmail (whitelist fail vs block list), and that `record.errors[:email]` contains the expected key.

findings.title: Email validation does a DB write on every blocked-email hit
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is invoked from `validate_each`, which runs on every user save when the email changes. Each call performs a SELECT plus an UPDATE to track statistics. That makes a previously pure read-side validation write to the DB and, combined with the read-modify-write race above, turns user signup into a small thundering herd against `blocked_emails`. Consider tracking match stats out-of-band (background job, or only when not blocked by the domain check), or at minimum batching the write.
